questions.stem: A hostile competitive environment is best described as a market with:
options: rapidly growing demand and few businesses competing for it
strict government price controls that remove all competition in it
intense rivalry, price wars and aggressive moves by competitors
a single seller and no close substitutes for its products
questions.explanation: A hostile environment is one where rivals compete aggressively, often through price cuts, heavy promotion and new entrants. A single seller describes a monopoly, and fast-growing demand with few rivals is a favourable environment.

questions.stem: Which is a key challenge of operating in a hostile competitive environment?
options: customers who are unable to switch to any other supplier
demand that is rising faster than the business can supply
falling profit margins as rivals keep cutting their prices
too few competitors to compare the business's prices against
questions.explanation: Price wars and aggressive rivals squeeze margins, which is a common challenge in hostile markets. Customers in such markets can switch easily, which is part of what makes the environment hostile.

questions.stem: A national supermarket chain enters a regional Queensland town and undercuts the local independent grocer on everyday items. Which marketing response best suits the independent grocer?
options: match every price cut, even if it means selling below its own costs
stop all promotion to save money until the new rival leaves town
copy the chain's whole product range exactly so customers see no difference
differentiate through local produce, personal service and loyalty rewards
questions.explanation: A small business rarely wins a price war against a larger rival with lower costs, so differentiating on what the chain cannot easily copy is more sustainable. Selling below cost would drain its cash, and copying the chain gives customers no reason to stay.

questions.stem: Integrated marketing communications means that a business:
options: lets each department design its own advertising with no shared message
replaces all traditional promotion with paid search engine advertising
coordinates all its promotional messages so they are consistent across channels
uses only one promotional channel, such as television, for every single message
questions.explanation: Integrated marketing communications coordinates advertising, social media, public relations and other channels so they deliver one consistent message. It uses many channels, not one, and it is the opposite of uncoordinated messages.

questions.stem: In the 4Rs of integrated marketing communications, 'recognition' refers to:
options: rewarding customers with discounts for repeat purchases
building a long-term, two-way bond with each customer
making the message suit the needs of the target market
customers being able to identify and recall the brand
questions.explanation: Recognition is about customers knowing and remembering the brand, for example through a consistent logo and slogan. Rewards, relationships and relevance are the other three Rs.

questions.stem: A sports retailer sends running-shoe offers only to customers who bought running gear before, timed for the start of the running season. Which of the 4Rs is it mainly applying?
options: relationship
relevance
recognition
reward
questions.explanation: Tailoring the offer to customers' interests and timing makes the message relevant to them. Recognition is about brand recall, and reward is about giving customers benefits for their loyalty.

questions.stem: A Brisbane cafe chain's app gives a free drink after every eight purchases and a birthday treat. Which of the 4Rs does this mainly demonstrate?
options: relevance
rejection
reward
recognition
questions.explanation: Giving customers benefits for their purchases is the reward element. Recognition is brand recall and relevance is fitting the message to the customer; 'rejection' is not one of the 4Rs.

questions.stem: Relationship marketing focuses on:
options: making as many one-off sales as possible to brand-new customers each month
using price cuts as the main way to attract every new customer
selling to other businesses rather than to individual consumers
building long-term relationships so customers keep buying from the business
questions.explanation: Relationship marketing aims to keep existing customers loyal over the long term, because keeping a customer usually costs less than finding a new one. A focus on one-off sales is transactional marketing.

questions.stem: Why is relationship marketing especially valuable in a hostile competitive environment?
options: loyal customers are less likely to switch when rivals cut their prices
it guarantees that no competitor can ever enter the business's market
it allows the business to raise prices with no effect on its sales
loyal customers make it unnecessary to maintain product quality
questions.explanation: When rivals compete aggressively, loyal customers give a business a more stable base of sales. Loyalty reduces but does not remove sensitivity to price, and it depends on continued quality.

questions.stem: A hotel chain's loyalty program has 200,000 members, but members' average stays per year have fallen for three years while complaints about room quality have risen. What is the most valid conclusion?
options: the program cannot hold customers if the core service is not satisfying them
the program should be closed, as loyalty programs never affect customer behaviour
the falling stays prove members prefer cheaper rewards from rivals
the rise in complaints is unrelated to the fall in members' stays
questions.explanation: Rewards can encourage repeat purchases, but customers dissatisfied with the core service will still drift away, so the trends suggest quality must be fixed. Concluding loyalty programs never work, or that the trends are unrelated, goes beyond the data.

questions.stem: How are contemporary marketing strategies, branding and loyalty interrelated?
options: branding matters only when a business is in the seed stage of its life cycle
strong branding and personalised digital marketing build trust, which drives loyalty
loyalty depends only on price, so branding has no effect on repeat purchases
digital marketing replaces branding, so a business no longer needs a brand
questions.explanation: A strong brand builds recognition and trust, contemporary marketing such as personalised digital offers reinforces it, and together these encourage loyalty. Price is only one factor in loyalty, and branding matters at every stage.

questions.stem: How does a strong brand help a mature business maintain its market share?
options: customers will pay any price, so the business can stop monitoring demand
customers trust the brand, so they are less likely to switch to rivals
a strong brand removes the need for any further promotion or advertising
a strong brand allows the business to ignore what competitors are doing
questions.explanation: A trusted brand creates customer preference and loyalty, which protects market share against rivals. Brands still need promotion and monitoring of competitors, and customers' willingness to pay has limits.

questions.stem: A cosmetics brand adds an augmented reality feature to its app so customers can see how a lipstick shade looks on their own face. This is an example of:
options: an economy of scale gained from buying inputs in bulk quantities
an emerging technology used in a contemporary marketing strategy
traditional print advertising aimed at a mass market audience
a quality assurance process to certify the product's safety
questions.explanation: Augmented reality is an emerging technology that lets customers try products virtually, making the marketing more engaging. It is not print advertising, quality assurance or a cost saving from bulk buying.

questions.stem: Which is a risk for a business adopting emerging marketing technologies, such as artificial intelligence that personalises offers using customer data?
options: misuse or loss of customer data can damage trust and breach privacy law
the technology prevents the business from reaching younger customers
personalised offers always reduce the business's average sales revenue
the technology means the business can no longer use social media at all
questions.explanation: Personalisation relies on customer data, so poor handling risks breaches of privacy law and loss of customer trust. The other claims are false: such technologies often help reach younger customers and lift sales.

questions.stem: Research and development (R&D) in business involves:
options: recruiting new staff through online job advertising and social media
reducing a product's price to clear excess inventory quickly
investigating and creating new or improved products and processes
collecting payments from customers who have overdue accounts
questions.explanation: R&D is the systematic work of developing new or improved products, processes and technologies. It can support both marketing, with new products, and operations, with better processes.

questions.stem: A Queensland agricultural machinery maker in a hostile market spends 8% of its revenue on research and development each year. Which is the strongest justification for this spending?
options: new and improved products differentiate it from rivals and protect its market share
research and development cuts costs immediately, raising profit in the same year
spending on research and development removes all risk from its future products
research and development replaces the need to listen to customers' feedback
questions.explanation: In a hostile market, innovation helps a business offer something rivals do not, protecting its sales. R&D is costly and risky in the short term, and its results depend on understanding customers.

questions.stem: Total quality management (TQM) is an approach in which:
options: quality is improved once and then left unchanged for several years
everyone in the business is committed to continuous improvement for customers
quality is checked only by trained inspectors at the end of the production line
quality is the sole responsibility of the business's senior managers
questions.explanation: TQM involves every employee in continually improving processes to meet customer needs. Relying on end-of-line inspectors is quality control alone, and TQM is ongoing rather than a one-off fix.

questions.stem: What is the relationship between total quality management and long-term achievements through customer satisfaction?
options: TQM raises costs so much that customer satisfaction always falls over time
TQM focuses only on reducing staff numbers, so customers are not affected
customer satisfaction matters only in the first year after TQM is first introduced
continuous improvement keeps customers satisfied, building loyalty and reputation
questions.explanation: By constantly improving quality to meet customer needs, TQM builds satisfaction, repeat business and reputation over time. Its focus is on customers and processes, not on cutting staff.

questions.stem: A Brisbane electronics retailer has its repair processes independently audited and certified against a recognised quality standard. As part of its quality approach, this is:
options: quality assurance, which checks that the processes meet set standards
quality control, which inspects each finished repair for any faults
a loyalty program, which rewards customers for repeat purchases
outsourcing, which hands its repairs to another business to do
questions.explanation: Quality assurance checks that processes are designed and followed to meet standards, often through independent certification. Quality control inspects outputs for defects after they are produced.

questions.stem: Project management involves:
options: recruiting staff and processing the payroll of a business each fortnight
promoting a business's products only through social media advertising
planning, scheduling and controlling resources to finish a project on time and budget
managing all of the business's routine, day-to-day operations that never come to an end
questions.explanation: A project is a one-off task with a start and an end, so project management plans and controls its scope, time, cost and resources. Routine ongoing operations are not projects.

questions.stem: A Gantt chart is used in project management to:
options: rank a business's customers by the share of total sales that each one provides
compare a business's marketing mix with those of its two main competitors
group stakeholders by how much power and interest they have in a decision
show the tasks of a project against a timeline, including when each starts and ends
questions.explanation: A Gantt chart is a bar chart of tasks against time, showing their start, duration and overlap. Ranking customers relates to Pareto analysis, and grouping stakeholders is a power interest grid.

questions.stem: A store fit-out has four tasks: A (3 weeks) first; B (4 weeks) and C (2 weeks) can both start after A; D (5 weeks) starts after both B and C finish. What is the minimum time to complete the project?
options: 10 weeks
14 weeks
9 weeks
12 weeks
questions.explanation: The paths are A-B-D (3 + 4 + 5 = 12 weeks) and A-C-D (3 + 2 + 5 = 10 weeks). The longest path is the critical path, so the project needs at least 12 weeks; adding every task (14 weeks) ignores that B and C run at the same time.

questions.stem: In the store fit-out (critical path A-B-D, 12 weeks; other path A-C-D, 10 weeks), task C is delayed by one week. What is the effect on the project?
options: the project is delayed by one week, because every task is on the critical path
the project is delayed by two weeks, because task C is twice as long as A
the project finishes a week early, because task D can start before task C
none, because task C has two weeks of float before it delays the project
questions.explanation: Task C is not on the critical path and has 12 − 10 = 2 weeks of float, so a one-week delay does not change the finish date. Only delays to critical-path tasks, or delays longer than the float, push the project out.

questions.stem: Outsourcing is when a business:
options: buys out a competitor at the same stage of production in its own industry
trains its own employees to take on tasks done by outside contractors
opens a new branch in another country that it owns and manages itself
contracts another business to carry out an activity it used to do itself
questions.explanation: Outsourcing hands an activity, such as call centres, delivery or payroll, to an outside provider. Buying a competitor is horizontal growth, and opening a branch it owns is not outsourcing.

questions.stem: A Gold Coast clothing brand outsources its social media marketing to a specialist agency. Which is the main advantage?
options: the brand no longer needs to set any marketing objectives of its own
access to specialist skills without employing extra full-time staff
complete control over every post the agency creates and publishes
the agency's costs will always be lower than doing the work in-house
questions.explanation: Outsourcing gives the brand expert skills and flexibility without hiring. It reduces direct control over the work, it is not always cheaper, and the brand still sets the objectives.

questions.stem: Which is a challenge faced by management when outsourcing marketing and operational activities?
options: keeping control of quality, confidentiality and the brand's reputation
finding enough office space for the outsourced provider's employees
having to pay the outsourced provider's staff under its own awards
losing the ability to cancel the contract under any circumstances
questions.explanation: Because another business does the work, managers must use contracts and monitoring to protect quality, confidential information and reputation. The provider employs its own staff in its own premises, and contracts normally include termination terms.

questions.stem: Economies of scale occur when:
options: the selling price rises because demand for the product increases
the average cost per unit rises because the business grows too large
the average cost per unit falls as a business increases its output
the total cost of production falls as a business increases output
questions.explanation: Economies of scale are falling average (per-unit) costs as output grows, for example through bulk buying. Total costs usually rise with output, and rising average costs from excessive size are diseconomies of scale.

questions.stem: A Queensland beverage maker has fixed costs of $200,000 a year and variable costs of $5 a bottle. What is its average cost per bottle at 20,000 bottles and at 50,000 bottles?
options: $15 at 20,000 bottles and $9 at 50,000 bottles
$10 at 20,000 bottles and $4 at 50,000 bottles
$15 at 20,000 bottles and $15 at 50,000 bottles
$25 at 20,000 bottles and $14 at 50,000 bottles
questions.explanation: At 20,000 bottles: $200,000 ÷ 20,000 = $10 fixed plus $5 variable = $15. At 50,000: $4 + $5 = $9. Spreading fixed costs over more units is an economy of scale; leaving out variable costs gives $10 and $4.

questions.stem: A national retailer pays less per television advertisement than a small rival because it books a whole year of advertising at once. This is a:
options: quality assurance process
joint venture agreement
marketing economy of scale
diseconomy of scale
questions.explanation: Buying advertising in bulk at a lower rate per advertisement is a marketing economy of scale. A diseconomy of scale is a rise in average costs as a business grows.

questions.stem: Pareto's principle (the 80/20 rule) suggests that:
options: about 20% of costs come from about 20% of products
about 80% of staff work about 20% of their hours
about 80% of results come from about 20% of causes
about 80% of customers buy only 20% of the time
questions.explanation: The principle holds that a small share of causes, such as customers or products, produces most of the results. In marketing it often appears as roughly 80% of sales coming from 20% of customers.

questions.stem: A Townsville office supplier finds that 150 of its 750 business customers provide 81% of its sales. Applying Pareto's principle, which marketing strategy is most sensible?
options: give those key customers extra attention and loyalty benefits
spend most of the marketing budget on its smallest customers
drop the key customers to reduce reliance on so few accounts
treat every customer identically regardless of their sales value
questions.explanation: The 150 customers (20%) give about 80% of sales, so protecting those relationships protects most of the revenue. Neglecting or dropping them would put most sales at risk.

questions.stem: A retailer finds that 20% of its product lines make 78% of its sales, while many slow lines take up shelf space. How does Pareto's principle help management of its marketing strategies?
options: spread promotion evenly, as every line contributes equally to the results
focus promotion and shelf space on the best sellers and review the slow lines
cut the best sellers, as they already sell well without any further support
add more slow-selling lines, as variety always raises total sales revenue
questions.explanation: Pareto analysis shows where most results come from, so the retailer can direct resources to its key lines and reconsider the slow ones. The data contradicts the idea that lines contribute equally.

questions.stem: In a STEEPLE analysis of a business facing a hostile market, a new state law banning certain single-use plastics would be classified as a:
options: sociocultural factor
technological factor
ethical factor
legal factor
questions.explanation: A new law is a legal factor in STEEPLE. Customers' changing attitudes to plastic would be sociocultural, and a business's own sense of right and wrong would be ethical.

questions.stem: A STEEPLE analysis for a Queensland budget airline shows: rising fuel prices (economic), a new low-cost rival (competition in the market), and growing customer demand for carbon offsets (sociocultural). What is the most valid implication for its strategic planning?
options: cost pressures and rivalry will squeeze margins, so efficiency and differentiation matter
the airline should raise all fares sharply, as every factor shown is an opportunity
the factors are unrelated, so the airline can safely respond to each one in isolation
the new rival means the airline should stop offering any carbon offsets to customers
questions.explanation: Higher fuel costs and a new low-cost rival both press on margins, while the carbon trend offers a way to differentiate, so the airline needs both efficiency and a point of difference. The factors interact rather than being isolated, and most are threats, not opportunities.

questions.stem: A unique selling proposition (USP) analysis compares businesses in order to identify:
options: how much power and interest each stakeholder has in a business decision
the driving and restraining forces acting on a proposed business change
the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats of a single business
what makes each business's offering different from those of its competitors
questions.explanation: A USP analysis compares the marketing mixes of competitors to find what makes each distinctive. The other options describe a power interest grid, a force field analysis and a SWOT analysis.

questions.stem: A USP analysis of three Brisbane gyms shows all three charge similar prices and offer similar equipment, but only one offers childcare. What is the most valid conclusion?
options: all three gyms have strong USPs because their prices are so very similar
the gym with childcare must lower its prices to match the other two
equipment is the main point of difference between the three gyms
childcare is a point of difference that can attract a distinct segment
questions.explanation: When price and equipment are similar, the childcare service stands out as the one gym's unique feature, attracting parents. Similar prices and equipment show the absence of a USP, not strong ones.
